sections.html:
Kuna is an Ada County city in the Boise metro area, with its business center about 18 miles southwest of downtown Boise. The 2025 estimate is 31,525 residents, up from 24,011 in 2020, 15,210 in 2010 and 5,382 in 2000. Few Idaho cities have grown faster. The 2020 census found a young, family-heavy place: a median age of 30.9, with 48.2% of households including children under 18.

Newer subdivisions now surround older farm lots. Canals and ditches cross the area, so a buyer's inspector may ask about irrigation rights, ditch easements and drainage on your lot. Part of Meridian lies inside the Kuna Joint School District 3, so ask which city and district apply to a specific address.

Kuna's growth comes from subdivisions replacing farms and ranches, and that shapes the resale market. The Kuna School District serves the city, parts of southern Ada County and a small portion of eastern Canyon County. It has more than 5,700 students and expects significant growth over the next 10 years based on approved developments.

A few rules around that growth are worth knowing:

  • Idaho does not allow school districts to require impact fees on developments.
  • In July 2022 the Kuna school board approved a voluntary contribution request of about $3,200 per housing unit, which developers may or may not pay.
  • School building bonds in Idaho need a 66 and two-thirds percent supermajority to pass.

For a seller, that means a steady flow of new homes competing with yours. A resale house in a neighborhood with active builders has to stand out on price and condition.

The City of Kuna handles building permits and planning through Development Services. The Building Department reviews plans and inspects every phase of construction and modification. Planning and Zoning is at 751 W. 4th Street, phone (208) 629-8853.

Projects usually go first to the Planning and Zoning Commission, which meets the second and fourth Tuesdays of the month. The City Council meets the first and third Tuesdays and has the final say on developments in the city.

If you finished a garage conversion, deck, shed or basement without a permit, a buyer's agent or lender may ask. Check with the Building Department before listing so an unpermitted item does not show up for the first time in an inspection report.

sections.h2: Property tax rolls, due dates and exemptions
sections.html:
Kuna's property tax is billed by Ada County. The main bill falls due December 20, with a split option that puts the second half on June 20. A fast-building city leans on the county's three tax rolls:

RollCoversBill sentDue
Primary (first half or full)Property assessed January 1 to the fourth Monday in MayNovemberDecember 20
Primary (second half)Second installment of the primary billNovemberJune 20
SubsequentProperty assessed fourth Monday in May to October 31JanuaryJune 20
MissedProperty assessed November 1 to December 31FebruaryJune 20

Extra bills can arrive if you occupied a newly constructed home or made improvements. Sellers of newer Kuna houses should ask the title company whether a subsequent or missed roll bill is still open, since it can come after the primary bill.

Assessment notices go out the first Monday in June, and appeals are due the fourth Monday in June. After that, the state process is to speak with the assessor, file with the Board of Equalization, then appeal within 30 days to the State Board of Tax Appeals or district court. The homeowner's exemption covers 50% of value, up to $125,000, for an owner-occupied primary home and up to one acre, and it ends when ownership changes. The Ada County Treasurer answers questions at taxinfo@adacounty.id.gov and 208-287-6800.

sections.h2: Disclosure when you sell in Kuna
sections.html:
Idaho Code 55-2504 makes anyone transferring one to four unit residential property fill out a property condition disclosure form. Sales, exchanges, installment contracts and options are all covered, as are rentals the owner does not occupy.

Section 55-2505 exempts some transfers: fiduciaries in an estate, foreclosures, transfers to a spouse or lineal relative, and newly built homes nobody has lived in. Sellers of those new homes must still state annexation and city service status. If you cannot tell whether you qualify, an Idaho attorney or title officer can say.

Many Kuna homes are recent builds, so drainage, irrigation and city services are the usual disclosure topics. Having answers ready speeds up any sale route.

sections.h2: Pricing a resale among new builds
sections.html:
A seller in a neighborhood with active builders competes with houses that have never been lived in, often with warranties and fresh finishes. The way to hold your ground is to know your own strengths: a finished yard, mature landscaping, an irrigation setup that works and permits for everything you added. Gather those documents before you set a price.

The 2020 census recorded a homeowner vacancy rate of 0.8%, which points to very little unsold inventory at that point. Conditions change, so ask a local agent about recent sales before settling on a number. A buyer who needs a loan may ask for repairs or credits after an inspection. A cash buyer does not need loan approval, so the condition of a house matters less to the timeline.

sections.h2: Preparing a Kuna house for sale
sections.html:
A short list handles most of what comes up. Ask the Building Department what permits are on file. Confirm with the title company whether any subsequent or missed roll bill is open. Write down how the lot is irrigated, where the ditch easements run and which school district and city apply.

  • Print the assessment notice and the latest tax statement.
  • Collect receipts and permits for any deck, shed, garage conversion or basement work.
  • Note your HOA status, if you have one.
  • Check occupancy: tell the buyer who lives in the house and when they can move out.

After closing, the settlement statement shows how the year's tax was split. File it with your tax records, since a late bill from a roll that was open at the time is easier to untangle with that paper in hand.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works for a Kuna house
sections.html:
Without a lender in the picture, the pace comes down to how ready you are and how quickly title work finishes. You request an offer and the buyer looks at the property. A title company then handles closing and settles any mortgage or taxes from your proceeds.

  1. List what you know: occupancy, liens, back taxes, HOA status and repairs.
  2. Compare the offer with listing costs, repair estimates and carrying costs such as utilities and taxes.
  3. Pick a closing date that fits your move.

Owners who reach for this route are often relocating, handling an inherited house, dealing with a tenant problem or facing repairs they cannot pay for. Declining an offer costs nothing, and a local agent can weigh in on a listing.

faqs.q: How many people live in Kuna?
faqs.a: The 2025 estimate is 31,525 residents. The 2020 census counted 24,011 and the 2010 census counted 15,210.

faqs.q: Which county collects property tax in Kuna?
faqs.a: Ada County does. The first half or full payment is due December 20, and the second half is due June 20 if the first half was paid on time.

faqs.q: Can I get an extra tax bill after selling a newer Kuna home?
faqs.a: It is possible. Ada County issues subsequent and missed roll bills in January and February for improvements or occupancy assessed after the primary roll, both due June 20, so ask your title company to check.

faqs.q: Does Kuna charge school impact fees on new homes?
faqs.a: No. Idaho does not allow school districts to require impact fees. The Kuna School District asks developers for a voluntary contribution of about $3,200 per housing unit.

faqs.q: Is a disclosure form required for a Kuna sale?
faqs.a: Usually. Idaho Code 55-2504 requires one for one to four unit residential property, with exemptions in 55-2505 such as estate and foreclosure transfers.
